narrative.text: Fig. 1, 'Digital adaptation kits representing health content within broader needs for digital health implementations'. Three boxes are joined by plus signs: HEALTH CONTENT (information aligned with recommended health practices or validated health content), shown with the cover of this kit; DIGITAL HEALTH INTERVENTIONS (a discrete function of digital technology to achieve health-sector objectives); and DIGITAL APPLICATIONS (ICT systems and communication channels that facilitate delivery of the interventions and content). An orange frame encloses the three, and dotted lines run from it to the highlighted 'Services and applications' cell of a Foundational Layer (ICT and enabling environment) below, whose other cells are leadership and governance, strategy and investment, standards and interoperability, infrastructure, legislation, policy and compliance, and workforce. Source: adapted from reference 14.

labels: Digital adaptation kits within the SMART guideline continuum
Digital adaptation kits within the SMART guideline continuum

between: Overview
Source: Adapted from (18).

narrative.text: Fig. 2, 'Digital adaptation kits within the SMART guideline continuum'. Five rows: L1 Narrative (narrative guidelines: evidence-based recommendations with implementation and data guidance); L2 Operational (digital adaptation kits: software-neutral documentation of operational and functional requirements such as personas, workflows, metadata, algorithms, minimum data sets and priority metrics); L3 Machine readable (structured software-neutral specifications, code, terminology and interoperability standards); L4 Executable (reference software that executes static algorithms and interoperable components); and L5 Dynamic (precision health models trained and optimised with advanced analytics). Each row passes through a vertical 'Localisation' bar to its country-implementation adaptation: national policies and procedures; localised requirements; localised machine-readable code and standards; localised static digital services within a digital health enterprise; and dynamic applications optimised for local outcomes. A blue arrow beside them runs from 'Paper systems' at the top to 'Smart digital systems' at the bottom. Source: adapted from reference 18.

between: Digital adaptation kit for immunizations
Fig. 3 situates DAKs within the broader set of resources for planning and implementing digital health systems.
The DAK for immunizations, in particular, should be used to inform the overall individual-level data and functionality needs of the immunization programme.
This is not restricted for use in an EIR, as the content requirements outlined in this DAK can also be used to inform the design of an immunization module within
an electronic medical record (EMR) system, for example. The data and functional requirements outlined in this DAK can be supported by multiple services and
applications, including for example, civil registration and vital statistics systems and logistics management information systems.

narrative.text: Fig. 3, 'Planning and implementing a digital health enterprise: phases, steps and resources'. Seven numbered phases, each with its steps: 01 assessing the current state and enabling environment; 02 establishing a shared understanding and strategic planning; 03 defining the future state; 04 planning the enterprise architecture; 05 determining health content requirements; 06 M&E of digital health implementations and fostering data use; 07 implementing, maintaining and scaling. Beside them a grid of tiles names resources for each phase, marked as PDF for print or online environment; among them the WHO-ITU national eHealth strategy toolkit, the Digital implementation investment guide (DIIG), WHO guideline recommendations on digital interventions, Open Health Information Exchange, TOGAF, and a highlighted tile 'WHO SMART guidelines: digital adaptation kits (this document) and machine-readable recommendations' in phase 05. Source: adapted from WHO (reference 1).

between: Digital adaptation kit for immunizations
Fig. 4. Overview of key immunization processes
Note: The grey box is not covered in this DAK.

narrative.text: Fig. 4, 'Overview of key immunization processes'. Two swimlanes. Vaccination location management holds A. vaccination location registration, G. resolve duplicate client records, H. resolve duplicate vaccination events, I. report generation, and a grey 'Supply chain management' box not covered by this kit. Vaccination location runs from Start through B. plan service delivery into a Service Delivery area: C. client registration, D. administer vaccine, then 'All vaccine series complete?'; yes ends the process, no leads to E. client reminder and 'Overdue for a dose?', where yes leads to F. defaulter tracing and no to the end. Each workflow box carries a subprocess marker.

basis.saw: Fig. 6, a single-lane process for planning service delivery

between: Digital adaptation kit for immunizations
Objective: To prepare for an immunization session, either at the vaccination location or done on an outreach basis (see Fig. 6). The primary difference if done as
outreach is that all equipment and vaccines must be properly packaged (cold box) for transport.
Note: There are opportunities to integrate an EIR with stock management systems to provide the health worker with automated views and stock alerts.
Fig. 6. Workflow B: plan service delivery business process
B. Business process for plan service delivery
Note: The Activity with subprocess in the grey box (4. Order additional stock) is not covered in this DAK.

narrative.text: Fig. 6, 'Workflow B: plan service delivery business process', in one lane (vaccination location, health worker). From Start: 1. review past vaccination records to estimate vaccines needed; 2. record details on planning sheet; 3. sufficient stock in immediate location? If no, 4. order additional stock (a grey subprocess not covered by this kit); then 5. get needed stock; 6. record stock taken; 7. assemble all needed materials for the immunization session; End.

basis.saw: Fig. 9, a two-lane reminder process between the immunization registry and the health worker

between: Digital adaptation kit for immunizations
E. Business process for client reminder
Objective: To send vaccine reminders and recalls to a client or caregiver notifying that the client is due, due on a future date, or past due for a vaccine (see Fig. 9).
This is typically done electronically and automatically.
For clients already electronically registered, the same process may also be used to notify them of a new vaccine that is available for which they are eligible. This
could include relevant disease specific vaccines (such as those for COVID-19 or seasonal influenza). This would be more of a notification than a reminder.
Fig. 9. Workflow E: client reminder business process

narrative.text: Fig. 9, 'Workflow E: client reminder business process'. Two lanes: electronic immunization registry, and vaccination location health worker. From Start the health worker does 1. define/evaluate criteria and 2. select notification method; the registry does 3. generate list of clients and 4. send notifications. Then 5. client shows up for vaccination? Yes leads to D. administer vaccine; no leads to 6. is another reminder needed? Yes loops back to step 1; no leads to F. defaulter tracing.

basis.saw: Fig. 11, a two-lane process for resolving duplicate client records

between: Digital adaptation kit for immunizations
G. Business process for resolve duplicate client records
Objective: To identify duplicate client records and consolidate them into one most accurate/suitable (best) record (see
Fig. 11). This may be a fairly complex process and is typically not done by health workers; however, they will need to identify potential duplicates if they come
across them.
Fig. 11. Workflow G: resolve duplicate client records business process

narrative.text: Fig. 11, 'Workflow G: resolve duplicate client records business process'. Two lanes: PCPOSS, and vaccination location health worker or system administrator. The PCPOSS does 1. flag client records for evaluation and 2. produce list of potential duplicate records; the person does 3. perform manual review and decides 4. can records be merged? Yes leads to 5. merge records in the PCPOSS; no leads to 6. mark as 'not a duplicate' or 'pending'. Both end the process.

basis.saw: Fig. 12, a two-lane process for resolving duplicate vaccination events

between: Digital adaptation kit for immunizations
Objective: To identify duplicate vaccination events within a client record and update into one event (see Fig. 12). Although it is typically the function of a PCPOSS
to alert the user of potential duplicate events, the amount of automation in the resolving of the duplicates will vary. In some systems, it can be done in a more
automated way, while in other circumstances it is preferable to have the health worker, or a trained system administrator, review and make decisions. Ideally,
duplicate events are flagged, and an alert is sent at the time they are entered so they may be dealt with immediately by the health worker and are not saved in a
PCPOSS. This process assumes duplicate records have been saved to the system.
Fig. 12. Workflow H: resolve duplicate vaccination events business process
H. Business process for resolve duplicate vaccination events

narrative.text: Fig. 12, 'Workflow H: resolve duplicate vaccination events business process'. Two lanes: PCPOSS, and vaccination location health worker or system administrator. The PCPOSS does 1. identify groups of vaccination events for evaluation; the person does 2. evaluate vaccination event records and decides 3. duplicate events? No ends the process; yes leads to 4. select the most accurate/suitable event record, then the PCPOSS does 5. update vaccination event records and 6. generate report of duplicate vaccination events, and the process ends.

basis.saw: Fig. 13, a two-lane process for generating reports

between: Digital adaptation kit for immunizations
Objective: To provide the ability to access and analyse data to improve immunization programme decision-making (see Fig. 13). This business process outlines the
general process to generate a variety of reports that are routinely needed by the system administrator, health workers and other partners.
Reports will be defined and set up initially in the system and are expected to be revised and updated as necessary. Reports can be individually generated,
automatically generated and/or even sent to other reporting systems. They may include dashboards, which are predefined summaries that are frequently
automatically updated. They will also include aggregate reports that are typically required to be sent from vaccination location to district.
Examples of reports include reports on coverage, reminder/recall, client list, vaccine uptake, vaccination by health worker and/or vaccination location, comparison
between district of residence and district of vaccination, list of refusals, stock consumption, wastage or any other ad hoc required information. Additional data
quality dimensions and indicators can be measured or assessed against defined standards to determine quality of data (34).
Fig. 13. Workflow I: report generation business process
I. Business process for report generation

narrative.text: Fig. 13, 'Workflow I: report generation business process'. Two lanes: vaccination location health worker, and PCPOSS. From Start the health worker does 1. define parameters for report; the PCPOSS does 2. generate report; the health worker does 3. high level review and decides 4. report acceptable? No loops back to step 1; yes leads to 5. analyse, and the process ends.
